title: Grade 7 Computer Science: Programming with Blocks to Text

learn: Block coding (like Scratch) uses snap-together blocks; text-based coding uses typed words and symbols.
Professional programmers use text languages like Python, JavaScript and Java.
Python is popular for beginners because it reads almost like English.
check: Python is popular for beginners because it...
lessons.try: Compare a block program and the same program written in Python.

learn: In Python, print("Hello, world!") shows a message on the screen.
Text in quotation marks is called a string.
Programs run line by line, top to bottom.
lessons.try: Write a program that prints three lines about yourself.

learn: Syntax is the set of rules for writing code; a missing quote or bracket causes a syntax error.
Python uses indentation (spaces) to group code.
Comments start with # and are ignored by the computer; they explain code to humans.
lessons.try: Find and fix three syntax errors in a short program.

learn: input("What is your name? ") asks the user to type something.
Store the answer in a variable: name = input("Name? ").
The input is always a string.
check: The value from input() is a...
name = input("Name? ") stores the answer in...
lessons.try: Write a program that asks for your favourite food and repeats it.

learn: Concatenation joins strings with +: "Hello, " + name.
f-strings insert variables: f"Hello, {name}!"
Strings can be repeated with *: "ha" * 3 gives "hahaha".
lessons.try: Make a greeting card program with f-strings.

learn: .upper() makes all capitals; .lower() makes lowercase.
len("cat") gives 3, the number of characters.
Strings are indexed from 0: "cat"[0] is "c".
lessons.try: Write a program that prints a word in capitals and its length.

learn: Integers are whole numbers (5); floats have decimals (5.0).
int("7") converts a string to an integer; float("2.5") converts to a float.
You must convert input before doing maths with it.
check: Before maths with input, you must...
lessons.try: Ask for two numbers and print their sum.

learn: + add, - subtract, * multiply, / divide.
// is floor division (whole-number result); % is the remainder (modulo).
** is exponent: 2 ** 3 = 8.
lessons.try: Write a program that converts minutes into hours and minutes using // and %.

learn: Python follows the order of operations: brackets, exponents, multiply/divide, add/subtract.
round(3.7) gives 4; round(3.14159, 2) gives 3.14.
Use brackets to make your meaning clear.
lessons.try: Build a tip calculator that rounds to two decimal places.

learn: if checks a condition and runs indented code only when it is true.
Comparison operators: == (equal), != (not equal), <, >, <=, >=.
A single = assigns a value; == compares.
check: Code inside an if runs when the condition is...
lessons.try: Write a program that says "Freezing!" if the temperature is below 0.

learn: else runs when the if condition is false.
elif ("else if") checks another condition.
Python checks conditions in order and runs only the first true branch.
check: else runs when the condition is...
lessons.try: Write a grade program: 90+ is A, 80+ is B, 70+ is C, else "Keep practising".

learn: and: both conditions true. or: at least one true. not: reverses.
if age >= 13 and age <= 19: means a teenager.
Combine conditions to make smarter programs.
lessons.try: Write a program that checks if a year is a leap year.

learn: A while loop repeats as long as a condition is true.
count = 1, then while count <= 5: print(count), count = count + 1.
Something must change inside the loop or it runs forever.
check: A while loop repeats while a condition is...
A loop that never ends is...
To avoid an infinite loop, you must...
lessons.try: Write a countdown from 10 to 1, then print "Lift off!"

learn: While loops are good for repeating until the user gives a correct answer.
Example: keep asking for a password until it matches.
A sentinel value (like "quit") can end a loop.
check: While loops are good for repeating until...
Which could be a sentinel value?
lessons.try: Make a guessing game that loops until the guess is right.

learn: break exits a loop immediately.
Counters track how many times something happens.
Accumulators add up a total: total = total + number.
lessons.try: Count how many guesses a player needs.

learn: A for loop repeats for each item in a sequence.
for letter in "cat": print(letter) prints c, a, t.
For loops are best when you know how many times to repeat.
check: For loops are best when you know...
A for loop repeats for each...
lessons.try: Print each letter of your name on its own line.

learn: range(5) gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
range(1, 6) gives 1 to 5. range(0, 10, 2) gives 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.
The end number is not included.
lessons.try: Print the 7 times table using range.

learn: A loop inside a loop is nested.
Nested loops can print grids and patterns.
The inner loop finishes completely for each step of the outer loop.
check: A loop inside a loop is...
The inner loop runs completely for each...
Outer loop 3 times, inner 4 times: total inner runs?
lessons.try: Print a triangle of stars with nested loops.

learn: A list stores many items: fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"].
Items are indexed from 0: fruits[0] is "apple".
len(fruits) gives the number of items.
lessons.try: Make a list of five favourite songs and print the third.

learn: .append(item) adds to the end; .remove(item) removes it.
fruits[1] = "kiwi" replaces the second item.
Lists can grow and shrink as the program runs.
lessons.try: Build a to-do list program that adds and removes tasks.

learn: for song in songs: print(song) visits every item.
Use loops to search, count or total list items.
sum(), max() and min() work on number lists.
check: A for loop over a list visits...
lessons.try: Find the highest score in a list of scores.

learn: def greet(): starts a function definition.
Indented lines are the function's body.
Call it with greet() to run it.
lessons.try: Write a function that prints a short poem, then call it twice.

learn: Parameters are inputs: def greet(name):
Arguments are the values you pass: greet("Ana").
Functions can take several parameters.
check: In def greet(name):, name is a...
lessons.try: Write a function area(width, height) that prints the area.

learn: return sends a value back from a function.
def double(n): return n * 2, then double(5) gives 10.
Returned values can be stored or used in expressions.
lessons.try: Write a function that returns the larger of two numbers.

learn: Python error messages show the line number and type of error.
NameError: a variable isn't defined. TypeError: wrong type, like adding a number to a string.
Read the last line of the error first.
check: Read the ___ line of the error first.
lessons.try: Cause three different errors on purpose and read the messages.

learn: Tracing means following code line by line and tracking variable values.
A trace table records each variable after each step.
print() statements can show values while the program runs.
lessons.try: Make a trace table for a short loop.

learn: Test with normal inputs, boundary inputs (like 0 or the highest allowed) and invalid inputs.
Write down what you expect, then compare with what happens.
Fix one bug at a time and test again.
check: At the edge of allowed values
lessons.try: Write a test plan for your grade program.

learn: Choose a project: a quiz game, a calculator, a story adventure or a simple data tracker.
Write what it should do (requirements) and sketch how it works.
Break it into small parts you can build and test.
check: Big projects should be broken into...
lessons.try: Write a one-page plan for your project.

learn: Build the simplest working version first.
Add one feature at a time and test after each.
Save versions so you can go back if something breaks.
check: After adding a feature, you should...
lessons.try: Build version 1 of your project.

learn: Demonstrate your program and explain how it works.
Ask users for feedback and note improvements.
Reflect: what worked, what was hard and what you'd do next.
lessons.try: Present your project and write a short reflection.
